chapter_theme: Songs at Thiruthanigai (திருத்தணிகை, 4 of 5): love-laments for a girl wasting with longing for Murugan, the poet's confessions of infatuation with women and courtesans, of book-babble and begging praise of patrons, and a death song that lets go of wife, children and goods before the buffalo comes; the praise turns on Valli, Vishnu as uncle, Parvati, Murugan as Siva's teacher and as Sambandar, and the hill of Thanigai.
structure_note: Four akam laments in another voice for a lovesick girl (285, 286, 294, 297); confessions of women and lovemaking (287, 289 to 291, 293, 295, 296, 299), with courtesans named by money in 287 and 299; 288 confesses book-learning without devotion, 292 begging praise of patrons, and 298 is a death song. 291 and 292 give most of their praise to Parvati.

285.reading: In the voice of one who watches over a girl, the singer says that with her pearl strings scorched and buried in the dust on her breasts, and Kama of the fish banner fierce against her, she has melted and lost all power to act; she asks that, without her chastity perishing, the dear girl be given back her senses so that she may sleep on her bed. The praise names Murugan who gives the gods of the kalpaka city their rights, who told the meaning of the Veda to the god of golden Kailasa, and whose single long vel destroyed the asura armies, at Thanigai of white conches and pearl-strewn fields.
285.nuance: This is akam poetry for a girl in love with the god, not the poet's own confession. கற்பழியாதே, that her chastity not perish, sets the girl's steadfastness against the love that is wasting her. The praise repeats Murugan the teacher of Siva: சுடர்பொற் கயிலைக் கடவுட்கு இசையச் சுருதிப் பொருளைப் பகர்வோனே. The opening lines (தெரிவைக் கரிவைப் பரவைக் குருகி) are hard to divide.

286.reading: Again for a lovesick girl, the singer tells how Kama's new lotus arrow, the south wind that makes her breasts pour fire, the women in the street who quarrel angrily over her, and the rising moon have left her helpless, sleepless and afraid on her bed, and asks Murugan to give her his kuravam garland. The praise names him easy of reach for the hill folk who sow millet, the Kumaresa who took up the vel and gave the gods their realm, and the one who went to the city of the gods' tree and embraced its Lady, at Thanigai of the red lilies.
286.nuance: உன் குரவைத் தரவேணும்: the girl asks for the god's garland, a classical token of the lover. தெருவில் பெண்கள் மிகக் கறுவிச் சண்டையிட is the town's gossip (அலர்) at its harshest, women in the street quarrelling over her. The திரு embraced in the city of the tree is probably Devayanai, Indra's daughter.

287.reading: The poet speaks of women who sway breasts like golden pots, babble bird-call arts so that the money in a man's hand passes to them, wear the pottu on the forehead and loosen the cloth about their small waists, and calls them base and worthless; he asks that the mind caught in the net of their eyes be made to cease. The praise names Murugan of Thanigai, Kumaresa gracious to Siva who wears crane feathers and datura, to the sound of drums, and the lord who rests his heart on the breasts of the hunter girl whose speech is like sugar and the three fruits, and who smashed the heads of the rakshasas.
287.nuance: கைப்பொருள் புக்கிடவே தான் புட்குரல் விச்சை பிதற்றும்: their sweet talk, likened to the cries of birds, is a skill for getting the money out of a man's hand. அக்கண் வலைக்குள் அகப்படு புத்தி: the eyes are a net. The song ends with வேளே, not பெருமாளே.

288.reading: The poet confesses that he has not learned to melt in praise of devotees who praise the golden feet, has not left the babble of books to praise Murugan with skill and an untroubled mind, and wanders always, born and acting out deeds whose seed was sown before; he asks whether a day will come when Murugan ends his lying in this base birth and gives him a little release. The praise names Murugan the peacock hero, son of the wise one who gave his left side to the daughter of the mountain, who dwells on Thanigai hill where knowledge, tattva and the three Tamils in word, meaning and sound are unfolded, and who embraces the hunter girl.
288.nuance: புத்தகப் பிதற்றை விட்டு: book-learning is the babble that stands in the way of praise, a confession of the learned rather than of the lustful. முத்தி சற்று எனக்கு அளிப்பது: he asks only for 'a little' release. The last lines of praise (வஜ்ரனுக்கு அமைத்த கைத்தொழுத்து அறித்துவிட்ட) seem to tell of Indra's hand, but the allusion is unclear.

289.reading: The poet says he befriends the delusion of women with fragrant hair, fruit-red mouths and foreheads like the half moon, without seeking the skill to sing Murugan's flower feet, and calls himself proud, without a shred of generosity, a miser, one who never comes to the shrine to bow; he asks to be given the company of those dear to Murugan. The praise names Vishnu, envoy for the king of the Kuru line, the dwarf, the lover of butter with Lakshmi on his chest and lord of the three gunas, as his uncle, and Murugan at Thanigai, life of the sea-girt earth.
289.nuance: The plea is for a place in the assembly of devotees (இனியார் தம் சபை), not for the feet alone. Among the self-reproaches, the miser who gives nothing (உதாரம் துணுக்கிலி லோபன்) stands out. One word (வன்பில஧முகன்) is corrupt.

290.reading: The poet describes women with mountain breasts, carp eyes, moon faces, peacock gait and cuckoo speech who melt the heart and loosen their clothes on the bed, and calls himself dross and a fool drooping in an incurable sickness of union; he asks whether a day will come when Murugan sets him in the state of refuge. The praise names the vel that pierced the Krauncha, the Kumara who joined the hunters' little girl, the gracious one who removed the troubles of the gods who took refuge, at Thanigai hill of groves.
290.nuance: கலவியில் துவள் பிணி தீரா: union itself is an incurable disease. கசடனைக் குண அசடனை: dross, and a fool in character, the stock self-abuse.

291.reading: The poet heaps names on women who gloss their faces, deceive, frighten with their eyes, steal and beguile in speech, and calls himself the witless, pathless servant who stared and was deluded and took the worm-filled body for a thing of worth; he asks that the six-faced Saravana appear with his peacock and vel, and that, singing poems in padigams night and day, he be given the one thing that comes to erase what Brahma wrote. Most of the praise is for Parvati, who dwells in the side of Siva who laughed and burned the triple cities, the fisher girl, the daughter of the Himalaya, Abhirami, Gauri, the one who raises dharma and gives Tamil, whose little son Murugan dances on the peacock at Thanigai.
291.nuance: விதித்தன் எழுத்தினை: Brahma's writing on the forehead, fate, which the 'one thing' (ஒருபொருள்) is asked to erase. புழுக் குடலைப் பொருளென மிக எணி: the confession is of valuing a worm-filled body. The long list of Parvati's names (வலைமகள், அபிராமி, பகவதி, கவுரி, அறத்தை வளர்த்திடு பரசிவை) is the heart of the praise; several of its compounds are hard to divide.

292.reading: The poet confesses that he has sung praises of poor men, likening them to the cloud, the sun, Kama, the bountiful son, Kubera, the kalpaka tree, Vishnu who saved the elephant in the crocodile pool, the six-faced Murugan himself, Arjuna and Meru, and walking from door to door; he asks that this begging end, that he reach the two feet, and that devotees come into austerity. The praise names Parvati of the Himalaya who with the mountain as bow burned the cities at Athigai in an instant, and Siva of the old Tamil who dances beyond Vishnu and Brahma, whose wealth Murugan is, and a battle in which the asuras' crowns were crushed, at Thanigai.
292.nuance: The list of comparisons is the patron-poem itself, quoted to be renounced; it even includes comparing the patron to Murugan (முகமும் அறுமுகம் உடையவன் இவன்), the god the poet should have praised. இரவு தவிர: the plea names begging. Several comparisons (முதிய கனன், சயில பகலவர்) are uncertain.

293.reading: The poet speaks of women with bound hair, refined speech and bright eyes, whose cloth sways over their breasts and whose waists are thin, and asks that, infatuated, he not wander daily on earth with those he embraced in bed, but that Murugan give him the paired lotus feet whenever he thinks of him on the stout peacock. The praise names Raghu-Rama, whose arrow felled the ten-headed one's crowned heads, and Vishnu who measured the world in a step, as his uncle, at Thanigai of fish-filled tanks and bending plantains.
293.nuance: நினைத்த பொழுது உன பதத்து மலரிணை அருள்வாயே: the feet are asked for at whatever moment he thinks of the Lord, a simple and complete plea.

294.reading: For a lovesick girl, the singer says that through the flowers shot by Kama with his sugarcane bow and the moon that rises from the sea scattering pearls, this golden creeper is wasting, and asks Murugan to come today to Thanigai, famed in every direction, so that she does not droop. The praise names the bright vel that pierced the northern mountain, the jewelled chest that melted embracing the hunter girl, and the feet kept in the heart of Siva who wears datura and the river, and the lord who cut down the one who opposed him in the sea.
294.nuance: இற்றைத் தினத்தில் வரவேணும்: the plea is that the god come today, as a lover is begged to come. The line எத்தத்தையர்க்கும் இதம் மிக்குப் பெருக்க is unclear.

295.reading: The poet describes lovemaking on the bridal bed, breasts thrilling, bangles chiming, hair loosened, speech faltering, eyes closing, faces sweating, clothes slipping and bodies made one as hearts melt, and asks whether he will gain Murugan's love so that the care of being tossed on the shoreless waves of union's pleasure ends. The praise names the vel that fought when the sea burned and the gods cried 'refuge', Siva who wears the moon, the river, thumbai, arugu and konrai in his matted hair as father, and Murugan at Thanigai hill where the five-headed serpent worships.
295.nuance: கலவி கரை அழி இன்ப அலை: the pleasure of union is a sea without shore, and what he asks for against it is love (நினது அன்பு), not escape. ஐந்து தலை அரவு தொழுகின்ற தணிமலை: a serpent's worship at Thanigai, probably the local legend of Vasuki.

296.reading: The poet gives a long and elaborate scene of lovemaking with women like lotus-peacocks on a bed sprinkled with agil, musk and rose water, according to the law of love, and asks whether, when strength, form and beauty have rotted in that pride, his hair has greyed and his body ripened and fallen, Murugan will not think of him and let him enter and stay in the one supreme light. The praise is a battle sung in drum syllables, at which the ancient Bhairavi's heart trembled in wonder, and Murugan dancing on the peacock at Thanigai.
296.nuance: உடல் ஒக்கப் பழுத்து விழும் அளவில்: the hour of death is pictured as fruit ripening and falling, and the goal as entering a light (பரம ஒளியில் புக்கிருக்க), not as reaching the feet. The praise is almost all rhythm syllables.

297.reading: For a lovesick girl, the singer says that by the waves beating on the sea and by Kama, firm in deceit, loosing his five arrows, this one creeper, soft as cotton and like a peacock, has her golden body marred and her heart on fire, and asks Murugan whether he will not think of her loneliness that is wasting her. The praise is a picture of Thanigai, its coconut and plantain groves where bees hum and peacocks dance, its springs full of blue lilies, where Murugan stands.
297.nuance: பொன்றும் தனிமையை நினையாயோ: the girl's loneliness, the pain of separation, is what she asks the god to think of. The praise is almost all landscape. The closing lines are garbled (லதனு஡டே, மலாணனும்) and their sense is uncertain.

298.reading: The poet asks that, before the fools who drive the goring buffalo bind him and call him away, his wife, his babbling children at the breast, his old mother, his town and land, the garden he kept, his house, gold, earned wealth and all the rest become alien to his mind, and that he be given the two feet that make one free so that he may draw near release. The praise names Murugan the bridegroom of the daughter of the four-tusked white elephant, the one who joined the hunter girl at Thanigai, whose vel shook the eight elephants and eight mountains of the directions, hard to reach for those who do not praise and easy for those who praise in pure Tamil verse.
298.nuance: The list of what must become alien (மனைச்சி, குதலை மக்கள், தாய்க் கிழவி, பதி, நாடு, தோட்டம், மனை, அத்தம்) is the whole household, given in order of nearness; the plea is detachment before death rather than rescue at death. The bride of the elephant (இபத்தின் பிடி) is Devayanai, raised by Airavata. One word (அசுருதிக்கு) is unclear.

299.reading: The poet confesses that, infatuated with women whose glances bewitch young men, he lost his wits, gave them all his money and became destitute with hunger burning in his belly, befriending one, quarrelling with another, chasing a third, and calls himself a wretched sinner; he asks for the noble character to sing Murugan's feet. The praise names Murugan who delights when the garland of Tamil spoken by Arunagirinathan is recited, the poet whose Tamil sent the Jains to the stake and brought back a woman's husband, and the vel that destroyed Sura's clan, at Thanigai with its spring of the one blue lily.
299.nuance: விரித்து அருணகிரிநாதன் உரைத்த தமிழ்: the poet names himself, and his songs as a garland Murugan enjoys. வெடித்த அமணர் கழுவேற ஒருத்தி கணவனும் மீள: Murugan is the Tamil poet who impaled the Jains and revived a woman's husband, i.e. Sambandar. The confession runs from infatuation to money to hunger, a sequence of ruin.

links.note: Both are laments for a girl in love with Murugan, with the moon, the south wind and Kama's arrows as what wears her down; 24 is a mother's grief, 286 adds the town's women quarrelling in the street and asks for the god's garland.
Both confess begging praise of patrons in the language of gods and clouds; 292 goes further, quoting the poet comparing a poor patron to the six-faced Murugan himself, the god he should have praised.

Tirumular says the women and children who ate from the house do not follow the dead; 298 asks for that knowledge in advance, that wife, children, mother and goods become alien to the mind before the buffalo comes.

The Naladiyar's wise renounce in childhood, knowing grey hair will come; 296 is the prayer of one who did not, asking even when his hair is grey and his body ripens and falls to be taken into the supreme light.
The Kural makes women of divided heart the company of those whom Fortune has left; 299 lives the sequence, infatuation, all money given away, then hunger burning in the belly.

The Kural's woman says the axe of desire breaks the door of restraint bolted with shame (காமக் கணிச்சி உடைக்கும் நிறையென்னும் நாணுத்தாழ் வீழ்த்த கதவு). 285 shows a girl melted and helpless under Kama's arrows and asks that her chastity not perish (கற்பழியாதே) while she is given back her senses. The song prays for the girl to be spared what the Kural says desire does.

The Kural's woman says her sickness grows with the town's gossip as manure (ஊரவர் கௌவை எருவாக) and her mother's words as water. 286 lists among the things that have left the girl sleepless and helpless the women in the street who quarrel angrily over her (தெருவிற் பெண்கள் மிகக் கறுவிச் சண்டையிட), beside Kama's arrow, the south wind and the moon. Both count the town's talk as a cause of the love-sickness, not just a result.

The Kural warns against women who weigh the profit and then speak of their own virtue (பயன்தூக்கிப் பண்புரைக்கும்). 287 says the courtesans babble bird-call arts precisely so that the money in a man's hand passes to them (கைப்பொருள் புக்கிடவே தான் புட்குரல் விச்சை பிதற்றும்). Both see the sweet speech as calculated for gain.

The Kural asks what learning is for if one does not worship the good feet of the pure knower (கற்றதனால் ஆய பயனென்கொல் ... நற்றாள் தொழாஅர் எனின்). 288 confesses he has not left the babble of books (புத்தகப் பிதற்றை விட்டு) to praise Murugan, nor learned to melt praising the golden feet. The song is the Kural's question answered in the first person.

The Naladiyar says that studying worldly books while leaving the books of wisdom is only clamour (கலகல கூஉந் துணை) and does not remove confusion. 288 calls book-learning babble (புத்தகப் பிதற்று) that keeps him from praise and from a mind free of trouble (கலக்கமற்று). Both name the noise of reading that does not end bewilderment.

The Tirumanthiram tells of entering the Lord's city with the devotees of his devotees and being welcomed. 289, after calling himself proud, a miser and one who never bows at the shrine, asks to be given the assembly of those dear to Murugan (உனக்கு இனியார் தம் சபை தாராய்). The song asks for the company that, in the Tirumanthiram, brings even the unworthy to the Lord.

The Kural's lover says that the jewelled woman is herself the cure for the sickness she causes (தன்நோய்க்குத் தானே மருந்து). 290 calls the drooping in union (கலவியில் துவள் பிணி) an incurable disease (பிணி தீரா) and asks instead for a place in the Lord's refuge. On the reading that the பிணி is union itself, the Kural makes union the remedy and the song makes it the illness.

The Kural asks what is stronger than fate, which gets there first whatever other way one devises (ஊழிற் பெருவலி யாவுள). 291 asks for the one thing that comes to erase what Brahma wrote (விதித்தன் எழுத்தினை தரவரும் ஒருபொருள்). If Brahma's writing is read as fate, the song claims there is something stronger than fate, which the Kural denies.

The Kural's woman says the pleasure of love is a sea (இன்பம் கடல்) and its pain greater than the sea. 295 describes union's pleasure as waves on a shoreless sea (கலவி கரை அழி இன்ப அலை) and asks for the Lord's love so that the care of being tossed on it ends. Both make love's pleasure a sea; the song finds the trouble in the pleasure itself, the Kural in the pain that follows.

The Kural's woman asks whether Kama, who works on one side only, does not see her misery and grief (பருவரலும் பைதலும் காணான்கொல் காமன்). 297 tells of Kama, firm in deceit, loosing his five arrows on a lonely girl and asks the Lord whether he will not think of her wasting loneliness (பொன்றும் தனிமையை நினையாயோ). Both turn the love-sickness into a question to one who should see it.

The Kural says that for those set on cutting off birth even the body is too much, so why any further ties (மற்றும் தொடர்ப்பாடு எவன்கொல்). 298 lists wife, children, old mother, town, garden, house and wealth and asks that all become alien to him before Death's men come, so that he may reach release (முத்தி வீடு அணுக). The song turns the Kural's rule into a plea, naming the ties one by one.

source_issues: Song 289: one corrupt character in வன்பில஧முகன் (line 10); the intended word is unclear.
Song 297: one corrupt character in லதனு஡டே (line 12), probably லதனூடே; also the unflagged garble மலாணனும் (line 15), perhaps மலரயனும்.
Song 299: unflagged garble மிக்முள (line 4), probably மிகமூள ('flares up').
Song 287 ends with வேளே rather than பெருமாளே; the shrine is named only in தணிக்குமரேசா.
